posts.caption: My brother-in-law came out Sunday in boots so new they still squeaked. At lunch he told the whole table he'd ridden at summer camp in 1989 and it all comes back. At 2 o'clock I walked her up to the mounting block and she stopped dead three feet short of it. She looked at him. She looked at his boots. Then she looked at me, the same look the vet gets when he says quick little poke. Nobody pulled on the reins and nobody argued. He held the lead rope and took pictures for the family group chat. Everyone went home happy.
posts.first: The last time someone told me they'd ridden a little, they climbed on from the wrong side and apologized to the horse. Out loud, twice. My mare stood through all of it like a statue in a church. I've loved her a little more ever since, and I still bring it up at Thanksgiving.

posts.caption: I do the last check at 9:30, after the dishes and before I let myself sit down. Water first, then hay, then the gate latch, then the water again because I can't remember if I looked. My husband says I could put up a camera and watch from the couch. I've thought about it. I'd still go out. He's twenty-six this year and meets me at the shed door every night like he was expecting company. Some nights I stand out there longer than the check takes. The water is always fine. I look once more anyway.
posts.first: The winter our heated bucket quit, I set an alarm for 2 a.m. and carried a kettle of hot water out in my nightgown and muck boots. He drank half of it while it was still steaming. I went back to bed with frozen ankles and no regrets at all.

posts.caption: The hay guy pulled in Saturday with 150 bales on a trailer that was not built for 150 bales. We set up the usual line. Him on the trailer, me on the stack, my husband in the middle narrating his lower back. Pudding was supposed to be in the paddock. He was not in the paddock. He was in the hay barn, parked in front of the stack with a bite out of the first bale and a stem hanging off his lip. We worked around him for two hours. He moved exactly once, to reach the second bale.
posts.first: My hay guy has delivered to me for eleven years and has never once let me pay the right amount on the first try. He rounds down, I round up. We stand in the driveway every June arguing over twelve dollars like it's a tradition, because by now it is.

posts.quote: Paid $85 for a riding lesson. The instructor spent the whole hour talking to my horse.
posts.first: She kept saying good boy, you're doing all the work, while I bounced around up there hunting for my left stirrup. To be fair, he did listen to her better than he listens to me. By the end I was wondering if I should just drop him off next week.

posts.caption: It was her first show in four years and my first in about eleven. We spent a week getting ready. Mane pulled, tail washed twice, my good show shirt let out a little at the seams. Then we walked into the ring, she spotted the judge's booth, and decided the whole class was about the judge's booth. We passed it sideways four times. When they called placings, we were last of seven. I picked up the ribbon and she lowered her head so I could clip it on her halter. We walked out like we'd won the whole thing.
posts.first: I still have the ribbon from my first show, a pale pink sixth place from 1983. It's pinned to the corkboard in my tack room. I've won nicer ribbons since then, but that's the only one that has moved with me from barn to barn.

posts.caption: Saturday my friend Linda finally took me up on it. I'd been inviting her out after dinner for years, and she showed up at 8:15 in white sneakers, which I let go. We set two camp chairs in the aisle with a thermos of cocoa. I turned off everything but the string lights. For a while she talked. Then she stopped. You could hear five horses eating, the cat walking a beam, the wind on the tin roof. At 10 she said she should head home. At 10:40 she said it again.
posts.first: My first winter with horses I bought a folding chair at a yard sale for two dollars and set it outside the stall. I didn't do anything in it. I just sat. Twenty-some years later it's held together with baling twine, and I still won't replace it.
